family_judgments.evidence: The MCQ admits a reasonable simple-past alternative while the constructed formats constrain the present-perfect target; thus the formats do not provide equivalent evidence.
In MCQ, pragmatic preference for present perfect over simple past becomes decisive, whereas constructed items directly require assembling the declared form.
All formats concern whether Maya completed sending the invitation by now.

criteria.evidence: Producing “Has Maya sent” requires present HAVE, participle sent, and inversion.
Lexis and active transitive clause structure are simple; no substantial additional production grammar is required.
The constrained blank requires the finite operator, subject, and participle rather than allowing a one-word lexical answer.
The fixed template ending “the invitation?” makes “Has Maya sent” the determinate target completion.
No solver-proposed unkeyed alternative was supplied, and the template sharply constrains the response span.
Success also depends on reading the completion-by-now contextual cue, but vocabulary and discourse burden are low.
The response slot requires the present-perfect polar-question sequence “Has Maya sent”.
The short dialogue introduces no material undeclared grammar in the required response.
A successful completion must realize HAVE inversion and the participle.
The fixed final turn and following object phrase determine the keyed response.
No solver-proposed unkeyed alternative was supplied; the response slot excludes additions such as “yet” after the verb phrase.
Dialogue tracking is a small nuisance burden beyond the declared grammar.
Option A displays all three operations, but selecting it is recognition and can be aided by eliminating visibly ill-formed C and D.
The options and prompt use accessible vocabulary and do not require additional target-side grammar.

B, “Did Maya send the invitation?”, is a grammatical and contextually reasonable way to ask whether the planned action happened; the learner can choose it without the target construction, while the instruction’s “best” wording does not rule it out robustly.
Both A and B can ask about completion of a sending event this morning; A better matches a present-result reading, but B is not an invalid question for the stated situation.
The response mechanism is selection among displayed options, so accepted option A covers the keyed response.
Pragmatic interpretation of “by now” is needed to prefer A over the otherwise reasonable simple-past option.
Writing the target requires present-perfect HAVE, participle sent, and polar-question inversion.
The requested subject, verb, and object are supplied and require no substantial additional grammar.
“Did Maya send the invitation?” is a viable yes/no question from the source sentence, although the explicit completion-now instruction favors the target.
The intended present-perfect reading is clear, but a simple-past question remains communicatively defensible without an explicit requirement to use the present perfect.
“Has Maya sent the invitation yet?” is linguistically and contextually reasonable for the stated by-now goal, but is unkeyed; its omission rejects a defensible full response.
Full-sentence production and punctuation add response burden beyond the three declared KCs.

summary: Reject: the MCQ is not determinate against grammatical simple-past B, and the transformation rejects the defensible “yet” question.
